interview_context.setting_or_workflow_context: Outpatient oncology clinic workflow with limited visit time and interest in patient-specific literature summaries for decision support.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: I've mainly used UpToDate for most of my time in medical training... it was nice to see how things were organized very differently with, like, clear sections. Here's the summary, here's the citations, etc.
segments.rationale: The participant contrasts the reports with a familiar reference tool and positively notes clear sections. In the same segment, the participant immediately frames use in a busy clinic day as potentially too time-consuming.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: the hard part is, on the spot, being able to suss through all the different citations to know which one's credible and which one's not... I liked... in the pink report, it has all the different rankings of citations
segments.rationale: The participant says citation appraisal is hard in real time and asks for credibility cues such as rankings, study type, and sample size. The participant also states they are not convinced enough to rely on the report alone.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: if we're able to take sections of all four of the different, colors you gave, and combine them, that actually would be helpful... I liked, in the pink one, the rankings.
segments.rationale: The participant explicitly proposes combining strengths from multiple report styles rather than choosing one unchanged format. The excerpt ties this preference to ranked evidence and a desire to see primary literature.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: I liked, overall, the red format, I think, the most. I liked having the bottom line of where it's what it's thinking... if there was a... link to just have all the citations somewhere in a ranking format... that would be nice.
segments.rationale: The participant clearly identifies the red format as preferred because it starts with the bottom line. They also suggests offloading citation detail into a separate linked ranked resource.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: I think the organization, and also I felt like the language was friendly, that anyone could follow along... I liked how I tailored it back to your patient.
segments.rationale: The participant praises both tone and structure and specifically says the report was easy to follow. The excerpt also highlights patient-specific tailoring as a valued feature.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: it kind of gave you steps of how to think... think about another appointment in so-and-so months, this lab test in so-and-so months... Concrete next steps... is helpful.
segments.rationale: The participant values prompts that translate evidence into follow-up actions and contingency planning. The same segment links those prompts to making shared decision-making easier in clinic.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: red just read to me, like, something I would do, because it was streamlined to how I like to see things... Blue was just kind of, like, in the middle... Pink, I like the ranking.
segments.rationale: The participant explains why the red report matched their preferred way of thinking while blue did not provide enough. Pink remains appealing for evidence ranking but seems incomplete without more interpretive guidance.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: I want to see the end value of, okay, you had this cohort study, you had this clinical trial, how many patients is the trial? Why did the trial not go through? Why was the trial ended early?
segments.rationale: This excerpt is a direct request for deeper evidence metadata, especially sample size and trial context. The participant frames these details as important for interpreting the literature.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: Yeah, I think the length was fine... Two pages is sufficient... I don't think having to have [IDENTIFIER] listed out to make it 4 pages long is necessary.
segments.rationale: The participant gives a concrete preferred length and explicitly rejects expanding the report into a much longer document. The quote contains a likely dictated or transcript artifact, so it is anonymized conservatively.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: there's an aspect of, I think helping even scribes who prep clinic notes would be very helpful... the question would... need to be phrased it in a way that a scribe someone who does not know the field is able to easily access this data
segments.rationale: The participant extends the use case beyond physicians to support staff preparing clinic materials. They also note a usability constraint: prompts or queries must work for someone without deep field knowledge.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: I liked the organization. I liked how it was able to quickly pop out an answer... I definitely see the utility of using AI informing, or at least supporting clinicians in their investigations.
segments.rationale: The participant reports that the tools performed better than expected and highlights speed plus organization as strengths. They define the role of AI as supportive rather than substitutive.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: They were all fairly open-minded, where it's a shared decision-making approach... I don't think I would... want AI to tell me, oh, here's how you should do something... I liked how I gave you different options
segments.rationale: The participant values reports that preserve clinician judgment and present options rather than directives. This segment directly states a boundary on acceptable AI autonomy.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: someone who had, like, the pink model, that'd be very helpful, because it kind of spits out all the major papers in the field
segments.rationale: The participant ties evidence-dense output to a specific kind of patient interaction, showing that preferred output may vary by audience. The statement also reinforces the value of a paper-forward mode.

themes.theme_name: Concise summary first, deeper evidence optional
themes.theme_definition: The participant repeatedly prefers a streamlined main report that starts with the bottom line, stays short enough for clinic, and gives optional access to ranked evidence detail elsewhere. This reflects a desire to balance speed with credibility rather than maximizing detail in the main view.

representative_quotes.quote: I liked having the bottom line of where it's what it's thinking

themes.confidence_basis: Repeated directly across several segments with concrete preferences about summary placement, page length, and optional citation access.

themes.theme_name: Evidence needs credibility cues to be clinically usable
themes.theme_definition: The participant does not reject citations; instead, they want them made easier to interpret through rankings, study-type labels, sample sizes, and trial context. Without these cues, the participant does not feel ready to rely on the tool during real clinical work.

representative_quotes.quote: being able to suss through all the different citations to know which one's credible and which one's not
how many patients is the trial? Why did the trial not go through?

themes.confidence_basis: This concern appears early and returns multiple times with specific requested additions.

themes.theme_name: Patient-specific framing and next steps make the report useful
themes.theme_definition: The participant especially values outputs that move from general evidence to the specific patient, then translate that into concrete follow-up actions and alternative pathways. That feature makes the tool feel more relevant to real clinic conversations and shared decision-making.

representative_quotes.quote: I liked how I tailored it back to your patient.

themes.confidence_basis: The participant provides several specific examples and revisits this idea in both report preference and AI-role discussion.

themes.theme_name: AI should support clinician reasoning, not replace it
themes.theme_definition: The participant sees clear utility in AI for organizing information and generating answers quickly, but sets a firm boundary against AI making the decision. The preferred role is to support investigation, framing, and discussion while leaving judgment to the clinician.

analytic_memos.summary: The participant sees genuine promise in AI-generated literature reports but views them as support tools rather than replacements for clinician judgment. The strongest positive reactions center on organization, readability, a clear bottom line, and patient-specific framing that leads to concrete next steps. The participant consistently prefers a streamlined summary-first format for routine clinic use, especially under time pressure. At the same time, the participant wants stronger credibility scaffolding around citations, including ranking, study type, sample size, and trial context. A recurring pattern is the desire to separate concise main output from optional deeper evidence access, rather than forcing both into one long report. The participant also sees a role for these tools in previsit preparation and even for scribes, provided the prompting process is usable by someone without specialty expertise. Overall, the participant is cautiously positive: impressed by utility and speed, but not yet ready to trust the tool independently of their own review.
tensions_or_tradeoffs: Brevity for clinic speed versus enough evidence detail to establish trust.
A single streamlined format versus different modes for different users or encounters.
Supportive option-framing versus overly directive AI recommendations.
General evidence summaries versus patient-specific actionable guidance.
